rv.q: There may be a reason Cymbeline isn’t staged that often. Shakespeare’s late play wields enough plot to sustain a Netflix series across several seasons.

The set design by Basia Bińkowska is elegant, too, and the performances are sharp. But this is a tricky play to pull off because of its many (too many?) fevered components. Maybe it is lesser performed for good reason, or perhaps this production, full of inspired ideas, does not anchor them down enough.

Best not to fret too much about consistency. It works, just; and there are some gains –  for instance Kemp-Sayfi finds an added anguish, akin to internalised misogyny, when Posthumus rails at female weakness on being duped by Pierro Niel-Mee’s opportunistic, voyeuristic Iachimo about Innogen’s infidelity.

Cloten wears a sleeveless T-shirt and has shaved temples and manic air of entitlement; he is blatantly bad news. Worse than him, though, is the Iago-like Roman rotter Iachimo (Pierro Niel-Mee, tremendous), who convinces the exiled Posthumus that he has seduced her wife.

The original version’s scheming Queen is replaced by a dithering Duke whose ineptitness only strengthens Cymbeline’s temperament by comparison. Innogen flees from her mother’s court disguised as a man muttering “I see a man's life is a tedious one.” Where Tang fails is wrangling the play’s black humour.

Failing entirely to charm her, Iachimo decides to lie anyway, causing Posthumus to order her maid-servant to murder Innogen. There are various other plots and sub-plots – an impending war between Britain and Rome which seems by the by, an evil Duke who wishes to insert his son, Cloten, into the royal family – but that’s the general gist.
